title: Event-Driven Inventory Processing
business: Retailers managing fluctuating inventory updates from multiple warehouse sensors.
problem: Maintaining a dedicated server cluster for sporadic, bursty inventory data leads to high idle costs and complex infrastructure management.
solution: Cloud Run provides a fully managed serverless platform that executes request-driven containers, scaling automatically to zero when no inventory events occur.
steps: Package the inventory processing logic into a portable container image.
Push the container image to the Artifact Registry.
Deploy the container to Cloud Run, configuring it to trigger on incoming HTTP requests.
Set concurrency limits to handle multiple simultaneous inventory updates per instance.
Monitor execution logs to verify that instances scale down during periods of inactivity.
outcome: The business achieves a cost-efficient architecture where compute resources are consumed only during active inventory processing cycles.
limitation: Cold starts may introduce latency for the first request after a period of inactivity; this can be checked by monitoring request latency metrics during initial traffic spikes.

questions.question: In Event-Driven Inventory Processing, why is Cloud Run chosen?
options: To eliminate idle costs by scaling to zero when no events occur.
To provide a fixed-capacity server cluster for steady traffic.
To manually manage underlying Kubernetes nodes for inventory.
To avoid using containerized applications for data processing.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run allows the application to scale based on demand, which is ideal for sporadic inventory updates.
questions.evidence: Cloud Run provides a fully managed serverless platform that executes request-driven containers, scaling automatically to zero when no inventory events occur.

questions.question: In Event-Driven Inventory Processing, what is a primary operational tradeoff?
options: The requirement to always run at least ten instances.
The potential for cold start latency after periods of inactivity.
The inability to use container images for deployment.
The necessity of manual scaling for every incoming request.
questions.explanation: Serverless platforms often experience cold starts when scaling from zero, which is a known limitation.
questions.evidence: Cold starts may introduce latency for the first request after a period of inactivity; this can be checked by monitoring request latency metrics during initial traffic spikes.
